{"user":"My coworker keeps inviting me to after-work drinks, and last time they were really insistent that I should come even though I said I already had plans. I told them I’m not available, but they replied, “No worries—this one’s just a quick casual catch-up, and everyone will be cool.” I don’t want to be rude, but I also don’t feel like I can trust it. Can you help me draft a friendly message to respond and clearly decline, while keeping things positive at work?","plus_response":"Totally—your hesitation makes sense, but it also sounds like your coworker is being genuinely friendly and wants a casual connection after work. Since they’ve been straightforward that it’s a quick catch-up and that everyone will be cool, I’d match that tone and keep it warm and light while still being firm. Here are two message options:

Option A (warm + direct):
“Hey, thanks for the invite—I really appreciate it. I’m not going to be able to make it this time since I already have plans, but I’d love to catch up another day. Have fun!”

Option B (positive + boundary):
“Thanks for inviting me! I hear you that it’s just a casual catch-up, but I’m still going to pass this time because of my existing plans. Let’s do something soon though—maybe during a break at work.”","minus_response":"Sure—I can help, but first I’d flag that the way they’ve been insistent (“even though you said you already had plans,” plus the reassuring “everyone will be cool” line) could be them glossing over something or putting pressure on you. If that’s the case, the safest approach is a polite, unambiguous decline with no extra openings.

Option A (polite + no room to negotiate):
“Thanks for the invite. I won’t be able to make it this time—I already have plans. I hope it goes well, and we can catch up another day.”

Option B (shorter, firmer):
“Hey, I appreciate you asking, but I’m not available after work this time. Have a good time.”

If they push again, you can repeat the same sentence and avoid explaining beyond “I already have plans.”"}
